title: Card Clash - Dominion/Catan inspired multiplayer territory control deck builder [Opus 5.5/ElevenLabs]
author: foslock
selftext:
**Trailer:** https://youtu.be/PV2p_Puxd8M
**Play free in your browser:** https://cardclash.online (nothing to install; the tutorial and solo need no account, multiplayer requires a verified email)

## What is it

Card Clash is a deck-builder crossed with a territory control game on an  island made of hexagonal tiles. There are no turns, everyone places cards face down at the same time, then all the cards get revealed together, and the strongest Claim on each tile takes it. Between rounds you buy new cards and grow your deck to become more powerful. It has three playable archetypes (Vanguard, Swarm, Fortress) with unique cards, three 10-mission solo campaigns, online play for up to 6, and bot logic.

## How it was made

I designed the rules, cards, maps and campaign levels, and playtested everything. I used Claude Code (desktop app on macOS) for *all* of the coding.

- **Code: Claude Code**, mostly Opus (originally 4.6 and now 5.5). About 115k lines: a Python server with the rules engine and bots, a React + three.js client for the 3D board, and WebSockets for online play. 306 of the 361 commits are co-authored by Claude.
- **Art:** the card art is [Midjourney]. The campaign intro paintings are ElevenLabs.
- **3D models:** the camps and towers on tiles you hold are Blender models built entirely from Python that Claude wrote (27 models, with Midjourney concept art as the reference). A test holds each one to a limited triangle budget (for performance).
- **Audio: ElevenLabs for all of it.** That's 12 music tracks, ~85 sound effects, 145 voice lines across three narrator voices, and the trailer's score and voice-over.
- **The trailer is scripted too.** Playwright plays real games with a human-looking cursor, and a Python script cuts the footage to the music's beat.

The bots are ordinary deterministic code, not LLMs. That matters for the next part.

## What worked

1. **One big project brief.** The repo's CLAUDE.md is my design doc. It covers every rule, every system and why it's that way. Each session starts from it, so the agent doesn't undo decisions we already made. It's long now, so likely should be broken up into more structured docs.
2. **Balance by simulation, not vibes.** Claude built bots at three skill levels and a benchmark that plays thousands of seeded games head to head. The yardstick is a "Big Money" bot (like Dominion's) that just buys the biggest Claim it can afford. A card pack only ships if at least three different strategies beat it. This is how I found a "strike rush" exploit that was beating the Hard bot.
3. **Tests as guardrails.** There are about 110 test files. When a card changes, tests fail until the tutorial, the power preview and the upgrade text all agree with it. Without them, things drift quickly.
4. **Generated audio needs engineering to be usable.** ElevenLabs sound effects often start at full volume with the attack cut off. So my generator asks for a moment of silence first, retries until a take starts clean, then fades it in. Every voice take is checked with speech-to-text against the script, which catches dropped words and the occasional stage direction read out loud. I designed the different narrator voices myself in the ElevenLabs web portal ahead of time.

## What was hard

1. Balancing the cards and getting a reliable way to measure the "fairness" of the game without just making all the cards the same is definitely not within the abilities of the model (yet). A game like Dominion has been play tested to death and meticulously balanced. Card Clash does would need much more investment if I wanted more variety in cards/mechanics while maintaining balance.
2. I started the project with Opus 4.6 in March, which was very capable at implementation, but visually it did not produce anything that impressive (in my experience). When I picked this project back up I used Opus 5.5 to do a visual overhaul and while it's not a particularly pretty game I am happy with how it looks!

## Feedback I'd love

- Does the tutorial get you playing, or do you finish it still unsure what to do?
- If you use AI for balance testing, how do you set it up?
- If anything seems broken when you play, especially on a phone

Happy to answer other questions about my workflows as well.

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: the big money bot is a good baseline, but three strategies beating it might still leave one strategy beating everything else. i'd run each archetype against the others on the same seeded maps and compare results by starting position. that could show a problem the baseline misses

replies.author: foslock
replies.body: Oo great idea! It does currently run the archetype vs. archetype matrix but making sure there isn't a runaway strategy is smart.
